metadata.title: PISA 2009 ASSESSMENT FRAMEWORK – KEY COMPETENCIES IN READING, MATHEMATICS AND SCIENCE

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This document describes the PISA 2009 assessment framework and administration design rather than an analysis with an explicit analytic dataset. PISA is implemented as a complex, multi-stage survey of 15-year-olds sampled within countries/economies and across schools, with rotated test booklets and background questionnaires; therefore, analysts using PISA microdata should apply the official student sampling weights and, where provided, replicate weights to obtain population-representative estimates and correct standard errors under the complex design. The framework text does not specify weight variable names (e.g., TOTWGT or W_FSTUWT) or replicate-weight methods, so those should be taken from the PISA 2009 Data File documentation. Plausible values are part of PISA’s achievement scaling approach in empirical cycles, but this framework report focuses on constructs, task design, and reporting scales rather than specifying PV combination or missing-data procedures for a particular model run.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This is a framework/assessment-design report that does not estimate predictive models on student-level achievement outcomes, so there is no analysis-specific plausible-values (PV) or missing-data handling strategy to report. The document explains how PISA reports proficiency using scales and how tasks are rotated across booklets, but it does not provide an empirical modeling section with PV combination rules or a documented missing-data procedure for an analysis. As a result, PV and missing-data handling are not applicable to the extraction of empirical ML methodology.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The report describes PISA 2009 as being administered to nationally representative samples of 15-year-olds in participating countries/economies, typically between 4,500 and 10,000 students per country from at least 150 schools, with rotated test booklets so that each student receives a subset of items. It also notes that the electronic reading assessment is implemented as an international option in a subset of countries/economies. No specific analytic inclusion/exclusion criteria (e.g., grade restrictions beyond age 15, item-completion rules, or missing-data exclusions) are provided because this is not an empirical analysis paper.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD report specifies the theory and operational design of PISA 2009, focusing on reading literacy as the major domain while also covering mathematics and science. It describes the assessment structure: paper-and-pencil tests administered over two hours with rotated booklets (13 clusters packaged into 13 linked booklets), plus an optional 40-minute computer-based assessment of reading and understanding electronic texts in a subset of participating countries. Outcomes are reported on proficiency scales (mean 500, SD 100) and, for reading, on subscales aligned to cognitive aspects (e.g., access/retrieve, integrate/interpret, reflect/evaluate) and text formats (continuous vs non-continuous), with additional reporting plans for electronic reading and potential cross-media scales. The report also details how background questionnaires for students and school principals (and sometimes parents) support contextual indicators. Because it is a framework document, it does not present model-based performance metrics or causal/predictive effects from an empirical analysis.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This extraction is sparse with respect to empirical ML and sampling details because the document is an assessment framework rather than a study that fits models to PISA microdata. It does not report an analytic sample size, per-country Ns, PV combination rules, missing-data handling, or any predictive modeling results; instead, it provides construct definitions, task design principles, and reporting scale plans. Therefore, fields like main_findings and ml_techniques are intentionally empty, and the remaining methodological content is captured in the survey/weighting interpretation and outcome summary.
